- All green things are blue.

Goal: derive Charlie is not blue.

We need to see if we can infer Charlie is blue or not. If we can't infer blue, then we cannot assert "Charlie is not blue" unless we can derive not blue via some rule (like something implies not blue). Typically we need to see if we can prove Charlie is blue; if we cannot, the statement "Charlie is not blue" may not be derivable (unless we have a closed world assumption? Not given). Usually we need to derive from given facts and rules whether the statement follows (i.e., is entailed). So we need to see if Charlie is not blue is entailed.

Thus we need to see if we can derive Charlie is blue from facts/rules; if we can, then Charlie is not blue is false (i.e., does not follow). If we cannot derive Charlie is blue, maybe we can derive Charlie is not blue via something else? Possibly from "If something is smart and not quiet then it is blue" but that's a conditional that gives blue if smart and not quiet. Not helpful for deriving not blue.

We have "All blue, furry things are smart." and "All blue things are smart." So blue => smart. Also "If something is smart and not quiet then it is blue." So smart & ~quiet => blue.

We have "All green things are blue." and "All green things are round." and "Furry things are green."

Thus: furry => green => blue (since green => blue). Also green => round.

Thus from Charlie is furry we can derive: Charlie is green (Furry things are green). Then Charlie is blue (All green things are blue). Also Charlie is round (All green things are round) – but we already have Charlie is round fact.

Thus Charlie is blue follows. Therefore "Charlie is not blue" is false; does not follow.

Thus answer: False.
